title: Count Friend Circles
statement:
There are n people, numbered 0 to n − 1. You get an n × n matrix knows where knows[i][j] = 1 means person i and person j are direct friends, and 0 means they are not. The matrix is symmetric and everyone knows themselves (knows[i][i] = 1).

Friendship links up into circles: two people are in the same circle if a chain of direct friendships connects them. Return the number of circles.

examples.why: 0 and 2 are friends. 1 knows nobody else, so 1 forms a circle alone.
Two pairs, {0, 1} and {2, 3}, with no friendship between the pairs.
0 and 2 are not direct friends, but both know 1, so the chain 0–1–2 joins them into one circle.

hints: Treat people as nodes and friendships as edges. What are you counting in graph terms?
Start a search from someone you have not visited yet. Everyone it reaches belongs to the same circle.
Count how many times you have to start a fresh DFS or BFS. Union-find works too: start with n groups and subtract one for every union that joins two different groups.

explain.intuition:
This is counting connected components. Each circle is a set of nodes connected by edges, and the matrix is just a different way of listing the edges: row i is the neighbour list of i, written as 0s and 1s.

Walk the people in order. When you meet someone not yet visited, they belong to a new circle, so add one and run a DFS that marks everyone reachable. Union-find gets the same count from the other direction: start with n separate groups and every friendship that merges two different groups lowers the count by one. A frontend analogy is grouping DOM nodes that share an event bus: anything connected by a chain ends up in one bucket.
steps: Create seen of size n, all false, and circles = 0.
For each person i not yet seen, add one to circles.
Run a DFS or BFS from i. From person u, visit every v with knows[u][v] = 1 that is not seen.
pitfalls: Counting direct friendships instead of circles. The third example has two friendships and one circle.
Treating the matrix as a grid and flooding over neighbouring cells. Cell (i, j) is an edge between people, not a land tile.
Union-find without path compression or union by size on large inputs. It still works here, but chains can make finds slow.

complexity.time: O(n²), since the matrix has n² entries

solutions.title: DFS from each unvisited person
solutions.idea: Every fresh DFS start is a new circle; the DFS marks everyone in it.

solutions.title: Union-find
solutions.idea: Start with n groups. Each friendship that joins two different groups lowers the count by one.

followups: Friendships arrive one at a time and you must report the circle count after each. Which approach fits?
The network has a million people with only a few friends each. How do you change the input format and the algorithm?
